argo.applications: Ocean heat content monitoring, seasonal forecasting, and short to long-range Numerical Weather Prediction, carbon budget, living marine resources assessment, ocean acidification study, oxygen minimum zone surveillance.
argo.coverage: Global ocean, from surface to 6,000 m depth.
argo.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Subsurface Temperature, Sea Surface Salinity, Subsurface Salinity, Subsurface Currents, Inorganic Carbon, Oxygen, Nutrients, Particulate Matter, Ocean Colour, Chla.
argo.implementationProgress: 56% of the target array (4,700 floats) achieved.
argo.platformType: Autonomous profiling floats: Core Argo (0–2,000 m), Deep Argo (to 6,000 m), and Biogeochemical Argo with biogeochemical sensors.
argo.activityTrend: Stable core array; BGC Argo expansion slowed due to funding constraints, with Deep Argo growth remaining limited. Polar expansion starting.
argo.challenges: Reliance on a limited number of contributors; funding gaps affecting BGC expansion; slow Deep Argo implementation; Exclusive Economic Zone deployment restrictions.
argo.opportunities: Argo BioEco and polar expansion through new technologies, including UVP plankton sensors, hyperspectral radiometry, and active acoustic observations, under ice communication.

dbcpMoored.applications: Weather forecasting, ocean forecasting, climate monitoring, satellite data calibration/validation, and climate and ocean science.
dbcpMoored.coverage: Tropical arrays across all ocean basins; coastal areas elsewhere.
dbcpMoored.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Subsurface Temperature, Sea Surface Salinity, Subsurface Salinity, Subsurface Currents, Sea State, Ocean Surface Heat Flux, Ocean Surface Stress, Surface Wind Speed and Direction, Surface Water Vapour, Surface Air Temperature, Air Pressure.
dbcpMoored.implementationProgress: ~500 moored buoys in operation; major coverage gap in the Southern Hemisphere.
dbcpMoored.activityTrend: Stable, but per latest governmental announcements probably shortly declining.
dbcpMoored.challenges: Deployment and maintenance currently concentrated in developed countries; limited capacity in developing regions. Buoys are reported as operational but without public data or metadata.
dbcpMoored.opportunities: Optimize ship time and coordination across observing networks to reduce deployment and maintenance costs.

goShip.applications: Heat and matter transport, decadal predictability, ocean carbon changes, ocean heat inventory, ocean ventilation, and anthropogenic carbon uptake.
goShip.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Subsurface Temperature, Sea Surface Salinity, Subsurface Salinity, Surface Currents, Subsurface Currents, Inorganic Carbon, Oxygen, Nutrients, Particulate Matter, Transient Tracers, Ocean Colour.
goShip.implementationProgress: Well implemented with decadal surveys since WOCE (1988).
goShip.samplingFrequency: Full-depth observations approximately every 30 nautical miles along ~50 repeated lines.
goShip.challenges: Increasing ship-time costs, including fuel costs, decarbonization targets and the need for research vessel fleet renewal.
goShip.opportunities: Optimize ship time and coordination across observing networks and participating institutes (multi-nation cruises).

dbcpTsunami.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Height, Ocean Bottom Pressure; some surface buoys also measure Sea Surface Temperature, Sea Level Pressure, and other parameters.
dbcpTsunami.platformType: Bottom pressure recorders with surface buoys.
dbcpTsunami.samplingFrequency: Every 15 seconds; data transmitted in real time during tsunami events.
dbcpTsunami.challenges: Public real-time data availability most likely lead to underestimation of activity trend.
dbcpTsunami.opportunities: Equip surface buoys with additional sensors to support other observing applications; improve synergies in ship time with other networks.

hfRadar.applications: Weather forecasting, operational ocean data and forecasting, climate projection, climate analyses and assessment, fundamental understanding of ocean processes, hazards response/early warning, sustainable management, area-based management tools, environmental assessment and outlook.
hfRadar.essentialVariablesMeasured: Surface Currents, Sea State, Ocean Surface Stress.
hfRadar.samplingFrequency: Most systems output a radial map of currents once an hour, but the temporal sampling could be increased to the order of five–ten minutes. The default sampling captures the diurnal cycle and above.

dbcpDrifting.applications: Weather and ocean forecasting, climate monitoring, satellite data calibration/validation, and climate and ocean science.
dbcpDrifting.coverage: Global ocean, between 60°N and 60°S, excluding marginal seas.
dbcpDrifting.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Surface Currents, Sea State, Particulate Matter, Surface Wind Speed and Direction, Surface Air Temperature, Air Pressure.
dbcpDrifting.implementationProgress: Close to 100% at global scale, but with too many drifters in the Atlantic and not enough drifters in other ocean basins.
dbcpDrifting.platformType: Surface Lagrangian drifters, typically equipped with a drogue centered at 15 m depth; other low-cost drifter designs are also being developed.
dbcpDrifting.challenges: High reliance on US funding (~75%); decline in surface pressure observations; drifter design constraints, including the use of drogues; instrument beaching and the need for recycling strategies; emerging private observing networks.
dbcpDrifting.opportunities: Develop drogue-free drifters for improved wind and wave observations; expand multi-variable observations; use more environmentally friendly materials, including wood and bioplastics.

gloss.applications: Sea level variability and rise monitoring, navigation and early warning systems.
gloss.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Level (Relative Sea Level and Geocentric Sea Level), Air Pressure.
gloss.implementationProgress: ~2,000 stations contributing in real-time, ~35% in the EU. More than 50% of the GLOSS Core Network (GCN: 300 priority locations) implemented; ~10% in the EU.
gloss.platformType: Fixed tide gauges and GNSS receivers (optional).
gloss.samplingFrequency: <1 min observations, hourly, daily and monthly means.
gloss.activityTrend: Increasing number of real-time stations. GCN implementation slowly declining.
gloss.challenges: Multi-purpose nature and diversity of data portals, data interoperability, and maintenance and training remain key challenges for ensuring long-term, high-quality datasets.
gloss.opportunities: Strong Member States contribution and international footprint and support for sustaining and developing observing capacity in developing countries.

oceanSites.applications: Climate reference stations (SITES) for physics, biogeochemistry and biology; including Meridional Overturning Circulation, ocean acidification, ocean warming and stratification changes, particle flux; air–sea carbon and gas fluxes; deep-ocean warming and freshening; satellite and Numerical Weather Prediction calibration/validation; ocean sound, full-ocean depth sampling.
oceanSites.coverage: Sites are operated in all global ocean.
oceanSites.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea State, Sea Ice, Sea Surface Height, Ocean Bottom Pressure, Surface and Subsurface Temperature and Salinity, Surface and Subsurface Currents, Oxygen, Nutrients, Inorganic Carbon, Particulate Matter, Phytoplankton biomass, Zooplankton biomass, Fish abundance, Marine mammal abundance, Benthic invertebrate abundance, Ocean Sound, Ocean Colour.
oceanSites.implementationProgress: Global design is guided by nations' priorities, depending on specific observing requirements (e.g. NWP cal/val); further representative flux reference sites are expected to improve predictions; ocean domain EOV time series and derived quantities (volume flux, heat flux, particle flux) sites extending over several decades.
oceanSites.platformType: Mostly moored and bottom mounted platforms; some ship-based operations all at fixed locations. Data is collected with autonomous physical, biogeochemical, ecosystem, geophysical sensors and samplers; ship-based sites also apply laboratory and experimental work.
oceanSites.samplingFrequency: From seconds to months (e.g. sediment trap); moorings typically recovered every 1–2 years.
oceanSites.challenges: Changes in national priorities on time series can lead to the loss of long-term time series and network capabilities; need for ship-time require long-term planning of operations.
oceanSites.opportunities: Cross-disciplinary ocean climate reference time series; network fosters international partnerships and collaboration on quality assurance, operational aspects, data management; collection of deep sea (>2,000 m) data as well as air–sea flux data. Climate site operations are often augmented with process studies and real-time data transmission to serve various ocean observing application areas besides climate.

gliders.applications: Boundary circulation; hurricane monitoring; global warming; the water cycle; sea ice; carbon cycling; anthropogenic impacts; and marine ecosystems.
gliders.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Subsurface Temperature, Sea Surface Salinity, Subsurface Salinity, Subsurface Currents, Inorganic Carbon, Oxygen, Nutrients, Particulate Matter, Ocean Colour, Ocean Sound.
gliders.implementationProgress: 58% of the target achieved (target: 100 gliders per day monitored).
gliders.challenges: Harmonizing data formats across platforms and regions; centralising data from multiple data endpoints; limited support for sustained ocean observing and technical coordination; limited coverage in the Southern Ocean; and restrictions on deployments within Exclusive Economic Zones.
gliders.opportunities: Increased collaboration across institutions; adoption of new sensor technologies; and integration of artificial intelligence methods.

anibos.applications: Ocean heat content; ocean forecasting; ocean variability; climate change; and biodiversity monitoring.
anibos.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Subsurface Temperature, Sea Surface Salinity, Subsurface Salinity, Oxygen, Ocean Colour.
anibos.implementationProgress: Excellent coverage in the Southern Ocean, but sparse coverage in other regions.
anibos.challenges: Fragile funding sources and high reliance on Australia, France, and the UK; incomplete data from the USA. Deployment is costly due to logistical challenges accessing remote field sites in the polar regions.
anibos.opportunities: Strong complementarity with Argo, particularly for observations in polar regions and a growing body of sensors deployed in the tropical seas that improve tropical storm and cyclone forecasting.

sotVos.applications: Global and regional Numerical Weather Prediction, forecasts and warnings to safeguard commerce and the protection of life and property at sea, climate monitoring, satellite data calibration/validation, and climate and ocean science.
sotVos.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Sea State, Ocean Surface Heat Flux, Sea Ice, Ocean Surface Stress, Surface Wind Speed and Direction, Surface Water Vapour, Surface Air Temperature, Air Pressure.
sotVos.implementationProgress: 75% of the target array (2,000 ships); ~1,500 operational voluntary ships reporting monthly and ~2,500 reporting annually.
sotVos.platformType: Manual or automated ship-borne weather stations; ~30% automated.
sotVos.samplingFrequency: Up to hourly for automated systems.
sotVos.challenges: Limited automation; resources required for data management and maintenance; low or stagnant funding from National Meteorological and Hydrological Services for marine observations.
sotVos.opportunities: Increased public/private investment, including the 10,000 Ships Initiative, with an aspirational target of 10,000 observing ships.

sotXbt.applications: Upper-ocean heat content monitoring, seasonal climate and ocean forecasting, ocean circulation monitoring in the upper ocean, and short-, medium-, and long-range Numerical Weather Prediction (such as El Niño).
sotXbt.coverage: Global ocean along selected reference lines.
sotXbt.implementationProgress: Well implemented against the target of ~30 reference lines sampled at least quarterly, but declining with declining funds.
sotXbt.platformType: Mostly automated XBT launchers deployed on commercial and research ships, often with a “rider” system.
sotXbt.samplingFrequency: 4–24 probes deployed per day during a cruise.
sotXbt.challenges: Frequently changing shipping routes and reduced funding.
sotXbt.opportunities: Optimize integration with other observing networks; maintain XBT observations in areas where Argo is not effective, such as boundary currents; sustain funding and existing reference lines to maintain the long-term record; facilitate access to ships of opportunity.

sotAsap.applications: Global and regional Numerical Weather Prediction, forecasts and warnings to safeguard commerce and the protection of life and property at sea, climate monitoring and prediction.
sotAsap.coverage: Primarily the North Atlantic Ocean, with sustained regional coverage.
sotAsap.essentialVariablesMeasured: Upper-air Wind Speed and Direction, Upper-air Water Vapour, Upper-air Temperature.
sotAsap.implementationProgress: Implemented to meet EUMETNET standards and requirements; no quantitative target defined.
sotAsap.platformType: Semi-automated sounding systems in 10-ft containers or portable launchers, primarily deployed on commercial vessels.
sotAsap.challenges: Complex logistics, particularly the return and handling of gas bottles.
sotAsap.opportunities: Adoption of hydrogen generator technology; expansion of ASAP network through the Global Basic Observing Network (GBON), a fundamental component of the WMO Integrated Global Observing System (WIGOS) designed to address geographical gaps in surface-based observational data.

fvon.applications: Ocean heat content monitoring, short- to long-range ocean–weather prediction, and support to the fishing industry operations, management, and research.
fvon.coverage: Coastal, shelf and shelf-break regions, boundary currents and frontal zones (0–1,000 m).
fvon.essentialVariablesMeasured: Subsurface Temperature, Subsurface Salinity, Subsurface dissolved oxygen.
fvon.implementationProgress: 9% of the target implemented and growing (target: 10,000 equipped fishing vessels by 2030); minimal implementation in the EU today. UK, Faroe Islands, and Iceland now all have sizable networks within the EEA.
fvon.platformType: Fishing vessels with their nets, traps, and lines equipped with oceanographic sensors so that profiles are performed during normal operations.
fvon.samplingFrequency: Minutes–hours during routine fishing. Variable based on fisheries, from hourly profiling to weekly.
fvon.challenges: Initial investment needed to expand FVON, particularly in Europe.
fvon.opportunities: Strong complementarity with Argo in coastal areas; potential for observations across EEZs; and opportunities to support ocean observing capacity in island and developing countries. Strong connection to fisheries sustainable resource management for livelihoods and food security.

smartCables.applications: Ocean circulation; ocean heat content; tsunami warning; deep-sea ecosystem monitoring; and marine mammal tracking.
smartCables.coverage: Currently none; regional systems are expected to develop over time.
smartCables.platformType: Submarine fiber-optic telecommunications cables with modular environmental sensor units.
smartCables.challenges: Developing network maturity and coverage; high deployment costs; national interests; and operational risks, including the inability to easily replace sensor modules.
smartCables.opportunities: Potentially longer sensor lifespans than those of other autonomous platforms; and the extensive reach of telecommunications cables across ocean basins.

soconet.applications: Greenhouse gas monitoring; global carbon assessments; air–sea carbon exchange; ocean acidification; and marine carbon dioxide removal.
soconet.implementationProgress: 66 platforms in 2025 (~30% of the initial goal of 200 active platforms). As an emerging network, SOCONET has not yet established an official implementation target.
soconet.platformType: Ship-based platforms, moorings, and uncrewed surface vehicles.
soconet.samplingFrequency: Varies by platform; typically hourly or more frequently.
soconet.challenges: Developing clear standard operating procedures and building capacity to improve measurement quality and entraining additional platforms; providing reference materials and intercalibration resources; conducting intercomparison studies to ensure measurement consistency across programs; and developing protocols for measuring other major greenhouse gases, including nitrous oxide (N₂O) and methane (CH₄).
soconet.opportunities: Integrating lower-cost, membrane-based pCO₂ sensors, which currently require further development to achieve the accuracy needed.

sunFleet.applications: Seasonal forecasting, short- to long-range Numerical Weather Prediction; tropical cyclones and hurricanes monitoring; carbon and ocean acidification; nutrients and biodiversity; surface fluxes.
sunFleet.coverage: Global deployments, with regional coverage and concentration in specific areas (e.g. TPOS) or during specific events (e.g. hurricanes).
sunFleet.essentialVariablesMeasured: Sea Surface Temperature, Subsurface Temperature, Sea Surface Salinity, Subsurface Salinity, Surface Currents, Subsurface Currents, Sea State, Ocean Surface Heat Flux, Ocean Surface Stress, Inorganic Carbon, Oxygen, Surface Wind Speed and Direction, Surface Water Vapour, Surface Air Temperature, Air Pressure.
sunFleet.challenges: Establishing formal governance structures for the emerging network; defining implementation targets; operating in Exclusive Economic Zones; and ensuring consistent data and metadata standards across manufacturers.
sunFleet.opportunities: Working directly with manufacturers to define data and metadata requirements; data buys vs platform ownership.

fvon.title: Fishing Vessel Ocean Observing Network (FVON)
fvon.paragraph1: With over four million fishing vessels operating worldwide, fishers are vital partners in complementing existing GOOS coverage and expanding ocean knowledge in under-observed geographies. "Fishing for data" in coastal, shelf, and other data-sparse waters is an opportunity to provide insights at a resolution and scale never seen before.
fvon.paragraph2: FVON's mission is to enable the transformation of fishing vessels into a collaborative fleet for inclusive and participatory data collection, worldwide. By connecting local fishing communities with global science, policy, and industry, FVON democratizes ocean observing and creates outcomes that matter: sustainable fisheries, accurate ocean forecasts, and robust coastal community resilience, supporting a data-driven ocean economy — where the benefits of ocean data are sustained and shared by all.
fvon.imageAlt: Fishing vessel with ocean observation equipment

smartCables.title: Science Monitoring And Reliable Telecommunications Subsea Cables (SMART Cables)
smartCables.paragraph1: Since the mid-19th century, subsea telecommunications cables have connected the world, enabling international calls, data transfer, and high-speed internet between countries. Today, the emerging SMART Cables network seeks to enhance this same infrastructure with a dual purpose — connecting people while advancing climate monitoring and strengthening earthquake and tsunami early warning systems worldwide.
smartCables.paragraph2: By integrating temperature, bottom pressure, and seismic motion sensors into telecommunication cables, SMART Cables will enhance GOOS by closing critical deep-ocean observation gaps. This new generation of cables will provide reliable, real-time, long-term data, delivering novel insights into the state of the ocean and essential information for operational centers to save lives and monitor climate change.

soconet.title: Surface Ocean CO₂ Observing Network (SOCONET)
soconet.paragraph1: Over the past decade, the ocean has absorbed about 26% of annual human carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions, helping to limit climate change (Global Carbon Budget, 2024). However, ocean CO₂ uptake varies greatly across time and regions, and robust information on these changes is still lacking.
soconet.paragraph1WithLink: Over the past decade, the ocean has absorbed about 26% of annual human carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions, helping to limit climate change (Global Carbon Budget, 2024). However, ocean CO₂ uptake varies greatly across time and regions, and robust information on these changes is still lacking.
soconet.paragraph2: SOCONET, a new addition to the GOOS observing networks, will use a wide range of observing platforms to expand the number of high-quality surface water CO₂ measurements. These observations are critical for assessing ocean health and quantifying the ocean's role in mitigating increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations.
soconet.imageAlt: Ocean CO₂ monitoring equipment and platforms

sunFleet.title: Surface UNcrewed Fleet (SUN Fleet)
sunFleet.paragraph1: Observing the ocean surface is essential for understanding air-sea exchanges, climate regulation, and the health of marine ecosystems. Yet collecting this vital data remains a major challenge, particularly in remote areas and harsh weather conditions.
sunFleet.paragraph2: SUN Fleet, the most recent addition to the GOOS observing networks, brings together uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs) to help close these observation gaps. By coordinating different USV operators, SUN Fleet will strengthen GOOS's ability to autonomously monitor up to 26 Essential Ocean Variables in underobserved areas, ultimately leading to improved forecasts and actionable insights into the state of the ocean worldwide.

satelliteObservations.title: Satellite Observations
satelliteObservations.introduction: Satellite observations provide a global view of the ocean, complementing in situ measurements from global arrays, reference observatories and regional systems. They provide repeated observations of surface variables such as sea level, sea surface temperature and salinity, ocean colour, winds and many other key variables. They are essential for monitoring large-scale ocean processes, supporting ocean and climate forecasting, and detecting changes over time. Together, satellite and in situ observations underpin our record of global sea-level rise, one of the clearest signals of human-caused climate change, and are essential for monitoring the rapidly changing polar oceans, where harsh conditions and limited ship access make sustained in situ observations challenging.

platformModal.title: Essential Climate and Ocean Variables observed from space
platformModal.introduction: This document provides additional information on the adequacy, continuity, and requirements of satellite observations for each Essential Ocean and Climate Variable, as contributed by the satellite ocean observing community. It summarizes the current status and future outlook of satellite measurements for each variable, outlining key achievements, challenges, and planned missions.

sst.title: SEA SURFACE TEMPERATURE:
sst.description: Sea Surface Temperature (SST) satellite measurements are currently adequate towards marginal for the future.
sst.detailedContent: The GCOS target requirements for satellite SST are an accuracy of 0.05K over 100 km, a stability of 0.01K/decade over 100-km scales, a horizontal resolution of 5-100 km and an hourly to weekly temporal resolution. The temporal resolution requirement is met adequately. The increase in geostationary infrared (IR) sensors partially mitigates degradations in temporal-spatial coverage due to cloud cover. The importance of passive microwave (PMW) retrievals is especially seen when persistent cloud cover prevents IR sensor retrievals for days, issue of particular importance in the critical coastal areas. The accuracy requirement is adequately met for most of the open ocean but is only marginally met for regions where the accuracy is degraded. These include areas where IR observations are limited by persistent cloud cover, high atmospheric water vapor, or elevated aerosol loading (impacting IR observations); regions of high wind speeds degrade PMW retrievals; and the Arctic Ocean, where a lack of in situ data for algorithm development and validation results in decreased performance. These topics are still on-going research with regular updates to algorithms at all agencies. NOPP has funded a 5-year project, the Multi-Sensor Improved Sea Surface Temperatures for the Arctic to increase the amount of in situ data, through annual Saildrone cruises, and incorporate the new data into algorithm development. Saildrone should be considered a key component as it can provide validation for gradients in areas such as the Arctic and coastal/estuaries regions. The horizontal resolution requirement is met by products that combine IR and PMW derived SSTs. However, this is also both temporally and regionally dependent. In areas of persistent seasonal cloud cover (such as upwelling regions) the feature resolution is inherently reduced to 25 km (PMW resolution). Advancing cloud masking is directly related to resolving spatial and temporal features in coastal and regional areas, where high resolution is critical for air-sea coupling and relationships to biodiversity. This is now an area of active research, which includes improving cloud masks to avoid flagging good pixels and clouds. Improvements have been made in implementation of machine learning for improving cloud detection, specifically in coastal regions. New reprocessed MODIS products include improvements in cloud masking which should allow for improved horizontal resolutions. There is considerable ongoing work in improving the accuracy of ECOSTRESS on board the International Space Station to resolved high spatial resolution which is critical for implementation of SST in numerical simulations of air-sea coupling. Looking ahead, two ultra-high spatial resolution to be launched in the upcoming years: ESA's Land Surface Temperature Monitoring (LSTM) and CNES-ISRO TRISHNA missions, both targeting 50m of spatial resolution. GCOS also requires continuing the provision of best possible SST fields based on a continuous coverage mix of polar orbiting (including dual view) and geostationary IR measurements, combined with PMW coverage. Geostationary satellites are essential for resolving the diurnal cycle, not resolved with polar orbiting satellites. While early geostationary instruments (circa 2000) initially provided SST data with lower accuracy (~0.5 K), modern sensor generations have significantly closed this gap. Meanwhile, polar-orbiting IR instruments continue to provide highly accurate (~0.3 K or better) and high-spatial-resolution measurements at high latitudes. The anticipated reduction in polar-orbiting IR fleets toward a small baseline of core approved satellites has stabilized, ensuring foundational IR continuity. However, the continuity of the PMW SST record, which is critical for persistently cloudy zones like nutrient-rich coastal upwelling regions supporting major global fisheries, remains structurally vulnerable. The threat of a severe, prolonged global PMW data gap has been partially mitigated by the successful launch of JAXA's GOSAT-GW satellite (carrying the AMSR3 instrument) on June 28, 2025. Standard AMSR3 environmental data streams became fully operational in June 2026, transitioning responsibilities away from the heavily aging AMSR2 sensor. To maintain the long-term stability of these vital SST products, the practical and accurate harmonization of AMSR3 data relative to the AMSR2 record is highly desirable. Crucially, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS), the Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites (CGMS), and the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) promote strict Earth-monitoring principles. These core guidelines dictate that a suitable overlapping period between successive satellite systems must be deployed to adequately assess inter-satellite biases, account for orbital drifts, and preserve data continuity. For robust inter-calibration that addresses environmental biases across a full seasonal cycle, the Group for High Resolution SST (GHRSST) promotes a principle of at least 1 year of concurrent, overlapping observations. Despite the relief provided by AMSR3's deployment and the ongoing calibration period, long-term constellation vulnerability persists. Europe's highly anticipated Copernicus Imaging Microwave Radiometer (CIMR) mission, designed to establish permanent, high-fidelity polar and global PMW coverage, is currently scheduled for launch in 2029 (CIMR-A). As a result, the global marine and meteorological research communities continue to focus heavy development on advanced IR cloud detection and atmospheric correction algorithms to squeeze maximum utility from infrared sensors when cloud layers permit. Critical to accuracy of SSTs are the series of Along-Track Scanning Radiometers (ATSR). The ATSR dual-view capability allows for improved atmospheric corrections which are necessary to achieve the climate precision of 0.1K/decade. The ATSR capability is being continued with the Sea and Land Surface Radiometer (SLSTR) on board ESA's sentinel 3. US polar orbiting IR satellites include the Advanced Very High-Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), and the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). VIIRS is available through both the Suomi National Polar-Orbiting (NPP) and NOAA's N20. These three satellites maximize coverage and spatial resolution, especially in areas of persistent cloud cover. However, the decommissioning of MODIS could have impacts on the quality of high-resolution SST data. A critical issue is to continue the accuracy and resolution provided by the MODIS satellites. This will require resources for the proper calibration and integration of VIIRS in fulfilling the requirements set by MODIS over its 25 years. The development of improved cloud masking will also be impactful to future missions such as TRISHNA. The accuracy of the data indicate they are comparable to MODIS and present the capability to extend the MODIS climate data record.

sss.title: SEA SURFACE SALINITY:
sss.description: Sea Surface Salinity (SSS) satellite measurements are inadequate, moving towards marginal.
sss.detailedContent:
The GCOS target requirements for satellite SSS are an accuracy of 0.1 pss for 50 km spatial average and monthly mean, a horizontal resolution of 10-100 km, a daily to weekly temporal resolution and a 0.01 pss/decade stability. While the spatial and temporal resolution requirements are currently approximately met, the accuracy requirement is not met globally nor regionally. The accuracy of satellite SSS is currently about 0.2 pss on monthly time scales at low to mid latitudes. Uncertainties are much higher at high latitudes due to the much lower sensitivity to salinity at L-band in cold waters. Also, SSS retrievals are degraded within ~50–100 km of the coast and ~150 km of the sea-ice edge due to land/ice contamination.

The GCOS also requires ensuring the continuity of space-based SSS measurements. Currently, two satellite missions, SMAP and SMOS, both launched more than 10 years ago, are providing SSS measurements. There is currently only one European mission (CIMR A/B) that will provide SSS every 2 days at about 50 km, aiming to continue the satellite SSS record and improve the sampling and accuracy of satellite SSS measurements for polar oceans. It is scheduled to be launched in 2028 so there could be a gap of a few years with no SSS measurements at all.
sss.author: Author: Severine Fournier, JPL

seaLevel.title: SEA LEVEL:
seaLevel.description: Global and regional sea level measurements from satellite are adequate through 2030.
seaLevel.detailedContent: For global mean sea level, the current altimeters meet the accuracy requirement (2-4 mm global mean and 10 mm locally). The temporal (weekly to monthly) resolution requirement is met, and the spatial resolution requirement is not applicable to the global mean. The stability requirement (<0.3 mm/yr) is met by the satellites for any one year, even though this requirement was not part of their design (until the launch of Jason-CS aboard Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich (S6 MF) and B in 2020 and 2025 respectively). Subsequent analysis by the science team and comparison with a variety of other satellite and in situ observations ensures this level of accuracy, which is verified through comparison with tide gauges. Regional sea level is observed with an uncertainty of 10 mm over 50-100km and a horizontal resolution of 100 km. Although 1/4-degree (25 km) products exist, they do not contain information on scales smaller than about 100 km (data from S6 MF and S6B, launched end of 2020 and 2025 respectively, help with the spatial resolution but how much it helps remains under investigation). The required 10 km resolution is only met with SWOT that was launched at the end of 2022. However, SWOT only fulfills the weekly temporal resolution requirement in combination with Sentinel-6 and the other Sentinel altimeter missions, but this requirement will be met as long as SWOT continues to operate. The stability requirement (< 0.3 mm/yr (for grid mesh of 50-100 km)) for regional sea level is met by the Sentinel 6 mission. The global mean sea level record is not at risk of lapsing before 2030, the planned end of the current Sentinel-6 mission pair. However, past 2030, no follow-on reference mission has been approved or funded (Sentinel-6 Next Generation remains unconfirmed and unsecured), which threatens the long-term stability of the record. Several missions are currently operational or planned for the near term, including Jason-3, Sentinel-3, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, and Sentinel-6B, alongside two forthcoming missions: CRISTAL (launch expected 2028) and Sentinel-3NG Topography (S3NG-Topo, launch expected 2034).
seaLevel.author: Author: Severine Fournier, JPL

winds.title: WIND SPEED AND VECTORS:
winds.description: Wind speed and vectors measurements are inadequate.
winds.detailedContent: The GCOS requirements are 10 km for spatial resolution and 1h for temporal resolution. These requirements are not met as current datasets have a spatial resolution of 20-30 km (regardless of interpolation to a finer grid) and a temporal resolution closer to 6h on average, but there are often much longer gaps. As we move to regional forecasting applications, at very high resolution, we are even further from the desired observation characteristics. Also, the ability to sample near coastal winds and the diurnal cycle remains problematic. The World Meteorological Organization requires 3 scatterometers in coordinated orbits to obtain 90% coverage of the ocean at 6-hourly interval. Sampling across different 6-hourly intervals is a minimum requirement to resolve the diurnal cycle. Currently, there are enough scatterometers in orbit publicly delivering data to meet these requirements, but they tend to cluster in the similar orbits with near 6 AM/6PM equatorial crossing time, therefore not sampling the diurnal cycles as needed. Nor do they provide the additional observations recommended by the International Ocean Vector Winds Science Team Meeting (IOVWST) for the deep topics. Polarimetric radiometers such as Compact Ocean Wind Vector Radiometer (COVWR) and Weather System Follow-on (WSF) can contribute to global coverage, and COWVR's position on the ISS provided the additional tropical coverage much like RapidSCAT. COWVR was launched as part of US Department of Defense's STP-H8 mission in December 2021 and was decommissioned in late 2025. WSF-M1 was launched in 2024. Additionally, data availability remains an issue with Chinese and Indian instruments that could allow us to meet these requirements. The requirement for accuracy (0.5 m/s except at wind speeds >20m/s) is not met in the context of differences between individual observations and comparison data. Comparison of individual scatterometer and radiometer vector wind with buoy wind shows an overall root means square difference (RMSD) of 0.9 to 1.0 m/s. In fact, it is thought that the error of buoy winds is at the 0.5 m/s level, which accounts for only 25% of the RMSD. Moreover, the discrepancy between collocated individual in-situ and satellite wind measurement also includes the effect due to sampling differences (e.g., pointwise in-situ measurement versus satellite winds that represent the average of a typically 25-km footprint). Such sampling difference can be much larger 1 m/s in regions with small-scale wind variability (e.g., associated with mesoscale convective systems). Systematic errors in buoy observations have been found, for buoys with anemometer heights of around 3 m, that are a function of wind speed > 7.5 m/s and wave characteristics (wave height and wave age). Removing these buoys from intercalibration data sets may further reduce the RMSD. Post-COVID changes of 0.5 to 0.8 ms-1 in tropical Pacific Ocean buoy calibrations have recently been discovered. Preliminary comparisons to other in situ platforms suggest that these changes are improvements. This error in the in situ observing system has led to an error in calibration of satellite winds that is still being assessed. The stability requirement is 0.05 m/s/decade. It has been published that we can detect 0.1 m/s/decade trends. It is not clear the goal of 0.05 m/s/decade is met year to year for all instruments but is close to being met with the ASCAT series of instruments. On decadal time scales and longer, the averaging of random error should be sufficient to meet the GCOS stability requirement. Further note that this requirement is applied to the ensemble of wind speeds. Such a claim cannot be made for some less frequently occurring ranges of wind speeds.
winds.author: Authors: Mark Bourassa, FSU; Tong Lee, JPL

seaIce.title: SEA ICE:
seaIce.description: GCOS requires sustained satellite-based (microwave radiometry, SAR, altimetry, visible and IR) sea-ice products. Satellite sea ice thickness measurements are marginal. Regarding sea ice concentration and sea ice drift measurements, they could become marginal in the future.
seaIce.detailedContent:
The GCOS requirements for sea ice thickness for temporal resolution (weekly) and spatial resolution (25 km) are met. However, the accuracy requirement of 0.1 m is not met with uncertainties remaining larger than 0.1 m. CryoSat-2 is planned to be decommissioned in 2028 when its successor CRISTAL is expected to launch. ICESat2 is in good health and expected to keep delivering data for years to come, therefore a gap in the record is not expected as long as ICESat2 is maintained.

Regarding sea ice drift, the temporal and spatial resolution requirements (weekly and 5 km) and the accuracy requirement (1 km/day) can be met using high resolution SAR imagery from Sentinel-1 and the RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) all year-round in the Arctic. The sea ice drift requirements are not met in the Antarctic, but this should change as ice drift products are developed using data from the recently launched NISAR.

For sea ice concentration and extent, the GCOS requirements for temporal resolution (weekly), spatial resolution (10-15 km and 1-5 km respectively) and accuracy (5% ice area fraction and 5 km respectively) are currently met but may not be in a near future if the continuity of observations is not guaranteed. If all planned sensors do not get successfully launched, a gap would preclude direct inter-calibration between sensors, which would reduce the quality of the overall time series.

The Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) missions that have provided very reliable microwave sea ice observations since 1978 have had substantially reduced support since April 2025 and not all data is being downloaded and processed; data provision may end at any time and thus the DMSP sources are no longer reliable. The DoD's WSF-M program (Weather System Follow-on Microwave; launched in April 2024) will help fill the potential gap ensuring the continuity of the long-term sea ice record from passive microwave.

The JAXA AMSR-2 sensor is still flying and AMSR3 was launched by JAXA June 2025. The CIMR mission has been approved and will be launched in 2028. The multi frequency microwave radiometer will provide sea ice concentration and sea ice extent at a spatial resolution of 5km with an uncertainty lower than 5% and sea ice drift at a resolution of 25 km.

The Metop-SG MWI instruments launch has been delayed until 2026 or 2027. These would complement WSF-M and fill potential gaps until CIMR is launched. The FY-3 series sensors are retrieving sea ice observations at a lower quality but as they are Chinese sensors, their access is restricted in the US. Thus, with overlap between nominally operating DMSP and the JAXA AMSR2 and WSF-M, sea ice concentration and drift can be extended at the DMSP quality level. WSF-M and AMSR2 overlap with AMSR3 will extend the higher resolution record (at least a full year of overlap for optimal inter-calibration has now been attained).

SAR sensors are extremely valuable as they allow monitoring of floating ice in all weather conditions. Current SAR missions are Sentinel-1, RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM), NISAR, SAOCOM-1, TerraSAR-X, COSMO-SkyMed, ALOS-2, SWOT, among others. Combining Sentinel-1 and RCM, and NISAR, key regions (i.e. Beaufort Sea, Fram Strait, Nares Strait) are monitored. It is important to ensure that future SAR missions include in their objectives the acquisition of data for operational detection of floating ice.
seaIce.author: Authors: Ted Maksym, WHOI; Stephen Howell, Environment and Climate Change Canada; Walter Meier, NSIDC

seaState.title: SEA STATE:
seaState.description: Sea State satellite measurements are currently inadequate.
seaState.detailedContent:
The GCOS requirement for the frequency (3-hourly) is met for most satellite altimeters. The requirement for uncertainty is of 5% but recent studies of comparison with wave buoys show the relative error from altimeters is roughly ~7-8%, which correspond to 16 to 22 cm for an average Significant Wave Height (SWH) of 2.5 m. The uncertainty is improved for recent satellite altimetry missions such as Sentinel-6MF, CFOSAT and HY-2B.

The preliminary results on SWH from SWOT nadir altimeter shows good relative error of 4.8% in comparison with other altimeters missions. The stability requirement of 1 cm/decade is almost reached with a stability close to 5 cm/decade. The largest weakness of altimeters are the frequency and the resolution. More missions in phased orbits are needed in order to get to 3-hourly and 25 km resolution (AltiKa like missions). Moreover, currently wave products from altimeters are available in less than 2-3 hours after sensing. This is consistent with the operational requirements.
seaState.author: Author: Lotfi Aouf, Meteo France

oceanColor.title: OCEAN COLOR:
oceanColor.description: GCOS requirements for ocean color remain adequate, though the sensor mix underpinning that assessment is in transition.
oceanColor.detailedContent:
The GCOS requirements for water-leaving radiance measurements call for a horizontal resolution of 4 km, daily temporal resolution, an accuracy of 5% (blue and green wavelengths), and a stability of 0.5%/decade.

Requirements for chlorophyll-a concentration call for a horizontal resolution of 4 km, weekly temporal resolution, an accuracy of 30%, and a stability of 3%. For most of Earth's oceans, these requirements continue to be met for both variables. Sentinel-3's OLCI instrument continues its 2-day revisit, 300-m ocean color record from Sentinel-3A and -3B, with a third unit, Sentinel-3C, planned for launch in October 2026 strengthening this contribution.

NASA's PACE mission, operating since February 2024, delivers global daily hyperspectral ocean color observations at 1-km resolution using its Ocean Color Instrument's 200+ spectral bands. On the multispectral side of the system, the MODIS instruments aboard NASA's Aqua and Terra satellites, which have been foundational to the ocean color climate data record since 2000 and 2002 respectively, are reaching end of mission. This removes two long-standing contributors to the temporal-resolution redundancy that has helped meet GCOS requirements.

VIIRS instruments aboard Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 are positioned to carry the multispectral role forward into the 2030s, with NOAA-22/JPSS-3 and NOAA-23/JPSS-4 to follow, but the loss of MODIS narrows near-term redundancy in the constellation. Looking ahead, two NASA hyperspectral missions are progressing toward launch to extend and diversify capacity: GLIMR and EAGLE-VSWIR (formerly Surface Biology and Geology).

GLIMR is estimated to launch as soon as 2027 and will be the first hyperspectral ocean color sensor operating from geostationary orbit. It will provide 300-m spatial resolution at nadir (roughly 1 km toward the edge of its field of regard) and will most frequently image the Gulf of Mexico at up to six times per day, with twice-daily or more coverage extending to the broader U.S. coastal waters, the Amazon River plume, the Caribbean Sea, and Hawaiian and South Pacific waters of interest.

EAGLE-VSWIR is a global 30-m hyperspectral imaging spectrometer on a 16-day repeat cycle slated to launch in 2028 or later. The ability to resolve coastal nearshore conditions remains a gap not explicitly covered by GCOS requirements. Multispectral land imagers such as Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 continue to partially fill this gap at finer spatial resolution, and a growing body of aquatic-tuned atmospheric correction and reflectance products is improving their utility for nearshore turbidity, suspended sediment, and chlorophyll-a retrieval. Once operational, GLIMR and EAGLE-VSWIR are expected to help close this coastal observation gap through sub-daily geostationary and higher-spatial-resolution hyperspectral measurements, respectively.

Commercial optical constellations are also increasingly contributing to ocean color capacity complementing the daily-global coverage of public missions. Planet's PlanetScope fleet provides near-daily, 3–4 m resolution multispectral imagery across most of the globe, including open-ocean as well as coastal and inland waters. However, these sensors have only four to eight bands limiting quantitative water-quality retrievals relative to dedicated ocean color sensors.

A newer generation of commercial hyperspectral operators including Pixxel's Firefly constellation (~5 m resolution, ~150 spectral bands) and Wyvern's Dragonette satellites (sub-10 m resolution) offer much higher spectral and spatial detail than PlanetScope but operate as narrow-swath (tens of km) with revisits over any given location depending on tasking priority rather than a fixed daily or weekly cadence. NASA's Commercial Smallsat Data Acquisition (CSDA) program is now evaluating several of these providers as potential complements to government ocean color missions.
oceanColor.author: Authors: Christine Lee and Amanda Lopez, JPL

introduction.paragraph1: GOOS biological and ecosystem observations, coordinated by the GOOS Biology and Ecosystems Expert Panel, are organized differently from those for ocean physics and biogeochemistry because of the distinct nature of the communities and complexity of the information needs. These observations are carried out by observing communities collecting data on the 12 biological and ecological Essential Ocean Variables (EOVs). These EOV communities bring together numerous independent monitoring initiatives worldwide to deliver the complex data vital to evaluate the status of marine life.
introduction.paragraph2: The GOOS BioEco portal provides an overview of the metadata available. The data itself can be sourced in the IOC Ocean Biodiversity Information System.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.intro: Short definitions for terms used throughout this GOOS Status Report. Filter by topic, then tap a term to read its definition.

goos.title: Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS)
goos.definition: The sustained, coordinated global system for ocean observations, designed to deliver the data and information needed for climate, operational services, and ocean health applications.

oceanops.title: OceanOPS
oceanops.definition: The operational monitoring and support centre for GOOS in situ networks. OceanOPS tracks platform activity, metadata, and network performance indicators used in this report.

inSitu.title: In situ ocean observations
inSitu.definition: Measurements taken in the ocean using platforms such as floats, buoys, ships, moorings, and gliders—as opposed to remote sensing from satellites.

eov.title: Essential Ocean Variable (EOV)
eov.definition: A variable identified by GOOS as critical for monitoring the state of the ocean and supporting science, services, and policy. Networks in this report are linked to the EOVs they measure.

goosPassport.title: OceanOPS passport
goosPassport.definition: Structured metadata describing a platform’s identification, affiliation, operation, hardware, and data endpoints. Metadata completeness indicators in this report are based on passport categories.

contributingCountry.title: Contributing country
contributingCountry.definition: A Member State or entity operating or funding platforms that feed operational data into GOOS networks monitored by OceanOPS. Counts follow the methodology described in the partners section.

operationalPlatform.title: Operational platform
operationalPlatform.definition: A platform in a mature network that meets network-specific activity rules and transmits near real-time data monitored by OceanOPS—shown on the map and counted in headline statistics.

referenceObservatory.title: Reference observatory
referenceObservatory.definition: Sites or lines delivering highest-quality reference, long-term, and often multidisciplinary observations in delayed mode to calibrate other systems and assess long-term change.

activePlatform.title: Active platform
activePlatform.definition: A platform counted as active for a network according to that network’s rules—for example, an Argo float that sent a profile within the last month, or a GLOSS tide gauge with a monthly mean within five years.

matureNetwork.title: Mature network
matureNetwork.definition: An established GOOS in situ network with operational monitoring by OceanOPS, widely adopted targets or self-declared status, and performance ratings in the networks matrix.

emergingNetwork.title: Emerging network
emergingNetwork.definition: A newer or developing GOOS network that is being integrated into the global system. Emerging networks may have limited OceanOPS monitoring or self-assessed indicators.

implementationStatus.title: Implementation status
implementationStatus.definition: A network performance indicator comparing operational activity to a community target, a self-declared target, or a self-assessed status when no target exists.

realTimeData.title: Real-time data delivery
realTimeData.definition: Timely transmission of quality-controlled observations to operational centres, including availability on the WMO Global Telecommunication System (GTS) and on the open internet with interoperable services.

archivedDelayedMode.title: Archived delayed-mode data
archivedDelayedMode.definition: Historical observations processed with additional quality control for scientific use (e.g. climate analysis), with raw data preserved and discoverable archives maintained.

metadataCompleteness.title: Metadata completeness
metadataCompleteness.definition: How fully platforms document methods, instruments, affiliation, and operation in OceanOPS metadata, averaged across selected platforms against network-specific criteria.

bestPractices.title: Best practices adoption
bestPractices.definition: The extent to which a network documents and shares harmonized practices across the observing lifecycle—from deployment and calibration to quality control, access, and archival.

deliveryClimate.title: Climate (delivery area)
deliveryClimate.definition: GOOS application area focused on climate monitoring, variability, and long-term change—including support for climate assessments and Earth system science.

deliveryOperational.title: Operational services (delivery area)
deliveryOperational.definition: GOOS application area supporting forecasting, safety, and marine operations through timely ocean observations and products.

deliveryOceanHealth.title: Ocean health (delivery area)
deliveryOceanHealth.definition: GOOS application area addressing marine ecosystems, pollution, and biodiversity through biological, biogeochemical, and ecosystem observations.

gts.title: Global Telecommunication System (GTS)
gts.definition: The WMO system for near real-time exchange of meteorological and oceanographic observations and forecasts among operational centres worldwide.

argo.title: Argo
argo.definition: Global array of profiling floats measuring temperature and salinity throughout the water column, coordinated as a core GOOS network.

vos.title: Voluntary Observing Ships (VOS)
vos.definition: Ship-based meteorological observations from participating vessels, supporting weather and climate services.

oceantrax.title: OceanTraX
oceantrax.definition: Ship-based oceanographic observations, including expendable bathythermograph (XBT) lines and related transect data.

goship.title: GO-SHIP
goship.definition: Global Ocean Ship-based Hydrographic Investigations Program—repeat hydrographic sections for full-depth reference measurements.

gloss.title: GLOSS
gloss.definition: Global Sea Level Observing System—coastal and island tide gauges for sea level monitoring and climate records.

oceansites.title: OceanSITES
oceansites.definition: Global network of multidisciplinary moored time-series reference sites in the open ocean.

mbn.title: Moored buoy network (MBN)
mbn.definition: Fixed moorings measuring ocean and atmosphere variables, including DBCP-coordinated moored buoys monitored for real-time delivery.

gda.title: Global Drifter Array (GDA)
gda.definition: Surface drifting buoys measuring sea surface temperature, pressure, and related variables as they move with ocean currents.

soconet.title: SOCONET
soconet.definition: Surface Ocean CO₂ Observing Network—platforms and sites measuring surface ocean carbon dioxide for climate and ocean health applications.
